fields.title: Haggai
fields.subtitle: Chaggai, “Festive”
fields.description: The tenth of the twelve Minor Prophets: four short messages, each dated to the day, given in 520 BC to the exiles who had come home from Babylon and left the LORD’s house in ruins while they panelled their own. “Think carefully about how you are living,” Haggai tells them: you have sown much and harvested little, and earned wages only “to put them in a purse with holes.” Unusually for a prophet, he was heeded at once. To builders discouraged by how small the new temple looked he brought the word “I am with you”, the promise that its glory would be greater than Solomon’s, and a signet ring for Zerubbabel. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Haggai about?
qa.answer: The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile. The Jews who returned from Babylon had laid its foundation and then stopped, saying the time had not come. In four dated messages Haggai calls them to rebuild (1:1–15), encourages them when the new house looks like nothing beside Solomon’s (2:1–9), teaches that holiness is not passed on by contact while uncleanness is, and promises blessing from that day on (2:10–19), and declares that God has chosen Zerubbabel as his signet ring (2:20–23).

qa.question: When did Haggai prophesy?
qa.answer: All four of his messages are dated to the second year of King Darius I of Persia, 520 BC: the first day of the sixth month, the twenty-first day of the seventh, and the twenty-fourth day of the ninth, twice. The book of Ezra records that Haggai and Zechariah prophesied together and that the people, encouraged by them, finished the temple in the sixth year of Darius, 515 BC (Ezra 5:1; 6:14–15). Nothing else is known of Haggai’s life.

qa.question: What does “Think carefully about how you are living” mean in Haggai?
qa.answer: It renders a Hebrew idiom, literally “set your heart on your ways”, which older Bibles translate “consider your ways” (1:5, 1:7). Haggai asks the people to look at the results of their priorities: they have sown much and harvested little, eaten and not been satisfied, and earned wages only to put them in a purse with holes, because they have built their own houses and neglected the LORD’s.

qa.question: How would the glory of the second temple be greater than the first?
qa.answer: The returned exiles thought their temple looked like nothing compared with Solomon’s (2:3). God promised to shake the nations and fill it with glory, so that “The glory of this house in the future will be greater than its glory in the past” (2:9). Christians have understood this as fulfilled when Jesus came to that temple and taught in its courts, and more widely in the church as the dwelling of God; Hebrews 12:26–28 reads Haggai’s promise to shake heaven and earth as pointing to the final kingdom that cannot be shaken.

qa.question: Why is Zerubbabel called a signet ring?
qa.answer: A signet ring was a ruler’s seal, his authority worn on his hand. Jeremiah had told King Jehoiachin (Coniah), Zerubbabel’s grandfather, that even if he were the signet ring on God’s right hand, God would pull him off (Jeremiah 22:24). Haggai 2:23 reverses that word for Zerubbabel, renewing God’s choice of David’s line. Zerubbabel was a governor, not a king, but he appears in the family line of Jesus in Matthew 1 and Luke 3, and Christians read the promise as reaching its goal in Christ.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Now be strong, Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. And be strong, all the people of the land, declares the LORD, and get to work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of Armies.

— Haggai 2:4

Haggai is the second shortest book in the Old Testament, and one of the most precisely dated. It holds four messages, each fixed to the day, all given within four months of the year 520 BC. And it records something rare in the books of the prophets: the people listened. Twenty-three days after Haggai first spoke, they were back at work on the house of the LORD.

The time

In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, and the next year he allowed the Jewish exiles to go home and rebuild the temple that Nebuchadnezzar had burned in 586. Some went. They rebuilt the altar and laid the foundation, and the old people who remembered Solomon’s temple wept at how small the new one would be (Ezra 3:12). Then opposition from their neighbours, hard times and plain discouragement brought the work to a halt. For about sixteen years the site lay unfinished.

Haggai spoke “In the second year of King Darius”, Darius I of Persia, to two leaders: Zerubbabel, the governor, a grandson of Jehoiachin, the last king but one of Judah; and Joshua, the high priest. The book of Ezra names him with his younger contemporary: “Now the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem” (Ezra 5:1). Encouraged by them, the people finished the temple in 515 BC.

Four messages

  • 1:1–15: “Think carefully about how you are living.” The first day of the sixth month: a call to rebuild, and the people’s response.
  • 2:1–9: “Be strong.” The twenty-first day of the seventh month, the seventh day of the Festival of Booths: the glory of the new house.
  • 2:10–19: “But from this day on I will bless you.” The twenty-fourth day of the ninth month: a question for the priests about holy and unclean.
  • 2:20–23: “I have chosen you.” The same day: a promise to Zerubbabel.

“Is it a time?”

The people had a reason for waiting. “The time has not come”, they said, “the time to rebuild the LORD’s house.” Haggai answers with a question:

Is it a time for you yourselves to live in paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?

— Haggai 1:4

Then he asks them to look honestly at their lives:

So now, the LORD of Armies says this: Think carefully about how you are living. You have sown much and harvested little. You eat, yet are never satisfied; you drink, yet never have your fill; you dress, yet no one is warm. And whoever earns wages earns them only to put them in a purse with holes.

— Haggai 1:5–6

A purse with holes: it is one of the Bible’s most vivid pictures of a life that works hard and gets nowhere. Haggai’s diagnosis is not that they were lazy. They were busy, “each of you hurries off to your own house”, but their priorities were upside down. God had been put last, and nothing else had prospered.

Then something happened that the prophets rarely saw. Zerubbabel, Joshua and “all the rest of the people” obeyed, “And the people feared the LORD.” Haggai’s next word is the shortest message in the book, and perhaps the most important: “I am with you, declares the LORD.” The LORD stirred up their spirit, and on the twenty-fourth day of the month they came and set to work.

The glory of the latter house

A month later, discouragement returned. The second message is spoken to those who could remember the first temple:

Who among you is still here who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Does it not look like nothing at all to you?

— Haggai 2:3

God does not pretend the new house is impressive. He tells them to be strong and work, because he is with them, as he promised when they came out of Egypt, and his Spirit still stands among them. Then he looks ahead: once more, and soon, he will shake heaven and earth and all the nations, and fill this house with glory.

The glory of this house in the future will be greater than its glory in the past, says the LORD of Armies. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of Armies.

— Haggai 2:9

The temple they built was enlarged by Herod into one of the wonders of the ancient world. But Christians have long seen the greater glory in something else: that Jesus himself came into that temple, taught in its courts and called it his Father’s house. The letter to the Hebrews quotes Haggai’s promise to shake heaven and earth “one more time”, and reads it as a final shaking, after which only “a kingdom that nothing can shake” will remain (Hebrews 12:26–28).

Holy and unclean

The third message begins with a question of ritual law. If holy meat touches other food, does the food become holy? No. If someone made unclean by a dead body touches it, does it become unclean? Yes. Holiness, in other words, does not rub off; uncleanness does. “So it is with this people”, says Haggai. A rebuilt altar did not make a people holy whose hearts were turned away, and their harvests had shown it. But now that they had turned, God makes a promise with a date on it: “But from this day on I will bless you.”

The signet ring

The last message is for Zerubbabel alone. God will shake the heavens and the earth and overturn the thrones of kingdoms, and on that day he will make Zerubbabel “like a signet ring, for I have chosen you”. A signet ring was a king’s seal, worn on the hand. Jeremiah had told Zerubbabel’s grandfather that even if he were the signet ring on God’s right hand, God would pull him off (Jeremiah 22:24). Haggai puts the ring back on. Zerubbabel never became a king; but his name stands in the family line of Jesus in both Matthew and Luke, and Christians read the promise as kept in the Son of David to whom it pointed.

How to read Haggai

Haggai can be read in ten minutes. Read it with Ezra 1–6 beside it, and with Zechariah 1–8, which was spoken in the same months. Notice the dates, and the call to “think carefully”, repeated again and again. And notice the order of things: first the honest look at one’s life, then obedience, then the promise “I am with you”, then the courage to keep going when the results look small.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Haggai are worth knowing.

“Think carefully.” The Hebrew says literally “set your heart on your ways”, which older Bibles render “consider your ways”. The translation gives the sense: “Think carefully about how you are living.”

“The LORD of Armies.” Haggai’s favourite title for God, used more than a dozen times in two chapters, renders what older Bibles call “the LORD of hosts”: the LORD who commands the armies of heaven.

“The wealth of all the nations.” In 2:7 the Hebrew word means what is precious or desired. The verb that goes with it is plural, so the translation reads it as the nations’ wealth, which verse 8 explains: “The silver belongs to me, and the gold belongs to me.” The Latin translation read it as a person, “the desired one of all nations”, and from it came the traditional “desire of all nations”, long sung of Christ.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Haggai 1
fields.body_html:
The house still lies in ruins

In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest: The LORD of Armies says this: These people are saying, “The time has not come, the time to rebuild the LORD’s house.”

Think carefully about how you are living

Then the word of the LORD came through the prophet Haggai: Is it a time for you yourselves to live in paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? So now, the LORD of Armies says this: Think carefully about how you are living. You have sown much and harvested little. You eat, yet are never satisfied; you drink, yet never have your fill; you dress, yet no one is warm. And whoever earns wages earns them only to put them in a purse with holes.

Go up and build the house

The LORD of Armies says this: Think carefully about how you are living. Go up into the hills, bring down timber, and build the house. Then I will be pleased with it and will be honored, says the LORD. You expected much, but it came to little; whatever you brought home, I blew it away. Why? declares the LORD of Armies. Because my house lies in ruins while each of you hurries off to your own house. That is why, because of you, the sky has kept back its dew and the earth has kept back its crops. I have called down a drought on the land and the hills, on the grain, the new wine and the olive oil, on everything the soil produces, on people and animals, and on all the work of your hands.

The people obey and begin the work

Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the rest of the people, did what the LORD their God said and heeded the words of the prophet Haggai, since the LORD their God had sent him. And the people feared the LORD. Then Haggai, the LORD’s messenger, gave the people the LORD’s message: “I am with you, declares the LORD.” So the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and that of everyone else among the people. They came and set to work on the house of the LORD of Armies, their God,

on the twenty-fourth day of the month, the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius.

fields.title: Haggai 2
fields.body_html:
The glory of this house

In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the LORD came through the prophet Haggai: Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the rest of the people, and say: Who among you is still here who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Does it not look like nothing at all to you? Now be strong, Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. And be strong, all the people of the land, declares the LORD, and get to work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of Armies. This is the promise I made with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit still stands among you. Do not be afraid.

I will shake the heavens and the earth

For the LORD of Armies says this: Once more, and soon, I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land. I will shake all the nations, and the wealth of all the nations will come in. I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Armies. The silver belongs to me, and the gold belongs to me, declares the LORD of Armies. The glory of this house in the future will be greater than its glory in the past, says the LORD of Armies. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of Armies.

A question for the priests

On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in Darius’s second year, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Haggai: The LORD of Armies says this: Ask the priests for instruction on this question: “Suppose someone carries consecrated meat in the fold of their garment, and the fold touches bread or stew, wine or oil, or any other food. Does that food become holy?” The priests answered, “No.” Then Haggai asked, “If someone who is unclean from contact with a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?” The priests answered, “Yes, it becomes unclean.” Then Haggai said, “So it is with this people and this nation in my sight, declares the LORD, and so it is with everything they do; whatever they offer there is unclean.” So now, think carefully about how things have been up to this day, before one stone was laid on another in the LORD’s temple: how, when someone came to a heap of grain expecting twenty measures, there were only ten, and when someone came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were only twenty. I struck you, and all the work of your hands, with blight and mildew and hail, yet you did not return to me, declares the LORD. Think carefully from this day on, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, from the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid. Think carefully: Is there still any seed left in the barn? Even the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate and the olive tree have not yet borne fruit. But from this day on I will bless you.

Zerubbabel, a signet ring

The word of the LORD came to Haggai a second time on the twenty-fourth day of the month: Tell Zerubbabel, governor of Judah: I am going to shake the heavens and the earth. I will overturn the thrones of kingdoms and shatter the power of the nations’ kingdoms. I will overturn chariots and their drivers; horses and riders will go down, each by the sword of his comrade. On that day, declares the LORD of Armies, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of Armies.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
On that day, declares the LORD of Armies, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of Armies.

— Haggai 2:23

Haggai ends with a promise to one man, and with three words, “I have chosen you”. The people who heard it were a small community of returned exiles in a province of the Persian empire, rebuilding a modest temple on a ruined hill. Nothing about them looked chosen. That is exactly why they needed to hear it.

The question the book leaves with you

Haggai’s first question is still the sharpest: “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” Every generation has its own reasons why the time has not yet come to put God first. Haggai does not argue with the reasons. He asks his hearers to look at what their own priorities have produced, a purse with holes, and to think carefully.

His second question is for those who did obey and were disappointed by the results: “Does it not look like nothing at all to you?” Here the book is very gentle. God does not tell them the work is greater than it looks. He tells them that he is with them, that his Spirit stands among them, and that the glory of the house does not depend on its stones. Faithfulness in small things, done in his presence, is not small.

Where it points

The promises of Haggai’s second chapter are larger than anything that happened in 520 BC. The shaking of heaven and earth, the wealth of the nations, the glory greater than Solomon’s, peace in this place, the chosen heir of David: the New Testament gathers them up in Jesus, who came to this temple, and in the “kingdom that nothing can shake” that he gives his people (Hebrews 12:28).

Where to go from here

A few places in this library to take Haggai further:

  • On courage for the work (2:1–9). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon Brave Encouragements, on Haggai 2:1–9; and the chapter “The Abiding of the Spirit the Glory of the Church” in Spurgeon on the Holy Spirit, on Haggai 2:4–5.
  • On the Spirit in the rebuilding. A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Days of the Restoration”, and his sermon Words for Discouraged Workers, which begins with Haggai and goes on to Zechariah’s visions.
  • On coming back to God. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, chapter “Ezra: Restoration from Backsliding”.
  • On putting God first (1:9; 2:8). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Morning by Morning, October 26, on Haggai 1:9, and Evening by Evening, August 4, on Haggai 2:17; and Faithful with Little, an Ochorus Original, chapter “It All Belongs to God”.
  • On what cannot be shaken (2:6). Hannah Whitall Smith’s The God of All Comfort, chapter “Things That Cannot Be Shaken”, on Hebrews 12:27.
  • On the greater glory (2:9). Augustine’s The City of God, Book XVIII, chapters 35 and 48, which argue that Haggai’s promise was fulfilled not in the rebuilt temple but in the church of Christ.

And read Zechariah 1–8 in this same edition, spoken in the same months to the same builders, and Hebrews 12.

Every reference to Haggai in this library can be tapped to read the verse. But the best next step may be to take up whatever work has been waiting, and to hear the word that was spoken to the builders:

This is the promise I made with you when you came out of Egypt, and my Spirit still stands among you. Do not be afraid.

— Haggai 2:5
